newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S., UK press on France over Iraq no-fly zone.
newsitem.headline: U.S., UK press on France over Iraq no-fly zone.

text.p: The United States and Britain agreed on Thursday they could patrol an extended no-fly zone over southern Iraq without France if Paris refused to drop its reservations about the operation against Saddam Hussein.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said after talks with British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind in London that he hoped France would overcome its coolness towards two U.S. cruise missile attacks against Iraq this week and join in policing the enlarged exclusion zone.

He then flew to Paris to meet French President Jacques Chirac and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette to try to iron out the most serious rift in the Gulf War coalition that drove Iraqi invasion forces out of Kuwait in 1991.
"I hope that after our conversations this afternoon that the French will go forward with the operations as we have had in the past," Christopher said before leaving London.
U.S. officials made clear that the no-fly zone extended by President Bill Clinton to the 33rd parallel, on the outskirts of Baghdad, could be patrolled even if France declined to go along.

"In discussions on the no-fly zone, they agreed that no matter what the French do, the U.S and the U.K. have the capability to implement effectively the no-fly zone," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"We've got sufficient air assets in the region to implement the extended no-fly zone."
Britain has strongly supported the United States in its decision to extend the limit from the 32nd parallel, where it was fixed after the Gulf War.

Rifkind took a veiled swipe at the French in a BBC radio interview, saying: "Those who criticise the Americans can only properly do so if they have an alternative strategy that would be more likely to deter Saddam Hussein from future aggression.
"Criticism of the Americans is easy, but coming from people who have not an alternative strategy it is far from convincing."

France played a key part in enforcing the initial no-fly zone. But it said on Wednesday its planes were staying south of the 30th parallel while it studied the implications of the unilateral American decision to extend the zone.
Christopher said the 33 cruise missiles fired at Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday had been an effective response to Baghdad after it sent troops into Kurdish regions of northern Iraq.
"I think we have brought home to Saddam Hussein that there is a very high price for the kind of repressive conduct that he has taken in northern Iraq," Christopher said.
"This is Saddam playing his old reckless game -- one which the international community has to stand up to or we will find him feeling that he has a licence to go on.
"The only kind of language he understands is the language of force," Christopher said.
Christopher welcomed Britain's "unstinting support" for the strikes and praised what he called the extraordinary partnership between Washington and London.

Referring to criticism by others, including Russia, China and most Arab states, he said: "We haven't always had support on the first day or the first week, but over time the world community has come to recognise and get behind those who show leadership to face up to the aggressors."
After his talks in Paris, Christopher was due to go to Germany, where he will meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl and deliver a lecture on European security.
